bib.title: Clean Code, Chapter 6: Objects and Data Structures
bib.venue: Prentice Hall (Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship)

question: When should state be hidden behind abstractions and when exposed as plain data, and what follows for coupling and change?
contributions: Objects and data structures are opposites, and each makes a different kind of change easy
Law of Demeter read through the object/data-structure distinction
Hybrids are the worst of both worlds; DTOs and Active Records should be treated as data

results.claim: Hiding implementation takes abstractions, not a layer of getters and setters.
results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured

results.claim: Procedural code makes it easy to add functions; OO code makes it easy to add classes.
results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured
results.quote: Procedural code (code using data structures) makes it easy to add new functions without changing the existing data structures.

results.claim: The complement: procedural code makes new data types hard, OO makes new functions hard.
results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured
results.quote: OO code makes it hard to add new functions because all the classes must change.

results.claim: Hybrids make both kinds of change hard and should be avoided.
results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured
results.quote: They are the worst of both worlds.

results.claim: Law of Demeter: chains through objects are a violation only if the elements are objects; for data structures it does not apply.
results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured
results.quote: Whether this is a violation of Demeter depends on whether or not ctxt, Options, and ScratchDir are objects or data structures.

results.claim: Fix for a train wreck on objects: tell the object to do the thing the caller wanted the internals for.
results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured
results.quote: If ctxt is an object, we should be telling it to do something; we should not be asking it

results.claim: Active Records should be treated as data; business rules go in separate objects wrapping them.
results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured
results.quote: The solution, of course, is to treat the Active Record as a data structure

results.setup: Java listings in Martin's chapter; argued, not measured
results.quote: Mature programmers know that the idea that everything is an object is a myth.

limits: Java-only listings; no measurement or evidence beyond argument
Footnote 1 concedes VISITOR/dual-dispatch work around the new-function cost but 'generally return the structure to that of a procedural program'
Bean/accessor framework demands (2008) are cited as a reason for the confusion; no mention of records, dataclasses or dynamic languages
Splitting train wrecks (Options opts = ...) is called a style fix, but the chapter says it does not resolve the Demeter question
practices: Do not add getters and setters automatically; design the abstract form of the data (p. 93-95)
Expose abstract terms (percent fuel remaining) rather than concrete storage (gallons) (pp. 94-95)
Pick objects where you add types, data structures plus procedures where you add functions (p. 97, 101)
Avoid train wrecks, i.e. long call chains [G36] (p. 98)
Tell objects to act instead of asking for internals (pp. 99-100)
Use DTOs at boundaries such as databases and sockets; treat Active Record as data and put business rules in separate objects (pp. 100-101)

terms.definition: Objects hide their data behind abstractions and expose functions that operate on that data. Data structure expose their data and have no meaningful functions.
a method f of a class C should only call the methods of C, an object created by f, an object passed as an argument to f, an object held in an instance variable of C; talk to friends, not to strangers
half object and half data structure: significant functions plus public variables or accessors (also called Feature Envy)
a class with public variables and no functions
private variables manipulated by getters and setters
a DTO with navigational methods like save and find, typically a direct translation of a database table
